title: 01. Foundations: Agent vs Chatbot vs Workflow Automation
summary: A Chatbot is a reactive system that responds to user messages in a single turn — it reads input, generates output, and stops. It has no tools, no planning, and no persistent memory beyond the conversation window.

sections.title: ① Concept Explanation
sections.body: A **Chatbot** is a reactive system that responds to user messages in a single turn — it reads input, generates output, and stops. It has no tools, no planning, and no persistent memory beyond the conversation window. **Workflow Automation** (e.g., Zapier, n8n) is a deterministic pipeline where actions are pre-defined and triggered by events — there's no LLM-based reasoning; the same input always produces the same path. An **AI Agent** is the union of both: it reasons like an LLM-powered chatbot AND takes actions like a workflow, but with dynamic, goal-driven decision-making that adapts to novel situations. The critical differentiator is **autonomy and adaptability** — agents can handle tasks not explicitly programmed. This distinction matters enormously in production because it determines the architecture, reliability profile, cost, and observability requirements of the system.

diagrams.title: Chatbot vs workflow vs agent — who decides the next step?
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart TB
  subgraph C["Chatbot"]
    c1["Prompt"] --> c2["LLM"] --> c3["Answer"]
  end
  subgraph W["Workflow - code decides"]
    w1["Step 1 fixed"] --> w2["Step 2 fixed"] --> w3["Step 3 fixed"]
  end
  subgraph G["Agent - LLM decides"]
    g1["LLM chooses action"] --> g2{"Done?"}
    g2 -- "no" --> g3["Run tool"] --> g1
    g2 -- "yes" --> g4["Answer"]
  end
diagrams.explain: The difference is **who controls the path**. A chatbot has one hop. A workflow has many hops but the **developer** hard-codes their order. An agent lets the **model** pick the next action at run time, so the number and order of steps is not known in advance. Use a workflow when the steps are predictable — it is cheaper and easier to test.

sections.title: ④ Visual Explanation
sections.body:
```
AGENT vs CHATBOT vs WORKFLOW AUTOMATION
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

CHATBOT                     WORKFLOW                    AI AGENT
───────                     ────────                    ────────
User ──► LLM ──► Answer    Step1 ──► Step2 ──► Done    User ──► [Loop] ──► Goal
  (single turn)              (deterministic path)         (dynamic, multi-step)

  ✅ Fast                   ✅ Reliable                  ✅ Flexible
  ✅ Cheap                  ✅ Predictable               ✅ Goal-driven
  ❌ No tools               ❌ No adaptation             ❌ Expensive
  ❌ No state               ❌ No reasoning              ❌ Hard to debug
  ❌ Can't act              ❌ No novel tasks             ❌ Non-deterministic

WHEN TO USE:
────────────
Chatbot:   FAQ, Q&A, simple lookup, customer queries
Workflow:  ETL, scheduled reports, deterministic pipelines
Agent:     Research, analysis, customer service with actions, coding assistants

HYBRID (RECOMMENDED FOR PRODUCTION):
─────────────────────────────────────

[Deterministic Steps]  ──────────►  [Agent Steps]
  OCR extraction                     Dispute resolution
  Data validation                    Content generation
  DB writes                          Ambiguous routing
  Email formatting                   Novel task handling
       ↑                                    ↑
  Workflow node                       LLM agent node
  (fast, cheap, reliable)             (flexible, expensive)
```

quiz.question: What are the three key dimensions that distinguish agents from chatbots?
options: No parallel actions — ReAct is strictly sequential (think → act → observe → think...); Verbose token usage — Repeating Thought/Action/Observation format consumes many tokens; Hallucinated observations — Without stop tokens, the LLM may fabricate observations.
The system prompt is the agent's constitution — it defines identity, capabilities, constraints, output format, and behavioral guardrails.
A thick agent encodes business logic in code (pre/post processing, routing rules) and uses the LLM only where judgment is genuinely needed — more predictable and cheaper.

Autonomy — Agents act without per-step human instruction; chatbots respond to every message; Tool Use — Agents call external APIs and tools; chatbots only generate text; Goal Persistence — Agents maintain a goal across multiple steps; chatbots answer one message at a time.
quiz.explanation: Autonomy — Agents act without per-step human instruction; chatbots respond to every message Tool Use — Agents call external APIs and tools; chatbots only generate text Goal Persistence — Agents maintain a goal across multiple steps; chatbots answer one message at a time ---

quiz.question: When would you choose workflow automation over an agent?
options: Yes — this is a common production pattern called Agentic Workflows.

Follow this 6-step design process: Define the goal space — What tasks will this agent solve? What's out of scope?; Identify required tools — What external capabilities are needed (search, DB, APIs)?; Design the memory architecture — Short-term (context window), long-term (vector store)?.

Use a risk-autonomy matrix: Low risk + high predictability → Full autonomy (no human in loop); High risk + high predictability → Human approval for specific action types; Low risk + low predictability → Agent acts, human reviews async.

Choose workflow automation when: Tasks are fully predictable and well-defined (same steps every time); Reliability is paramount (no tolerance for LLM hallucination); Latency is critical (no LLM inference overhead).
quiz.explanation: Choose workflow automation when: Tasks are fully predictable and well-defined (same steps every time) Reliability is paramount (no tolerance for LLM hallucination) Latency is critical (no LLM inference overhead) Cost is a constraint (no per-token charges) Choose an agent when: Tasks require dynamic decision-making based on intermediate results Input variety is high (many different phrasings/scenarios) The task…

quiz.explanation: Yes — this is a common production pattern called Agentic Workflows. Pre-defined steps that are reliable and deterministic run as workflow nodes; ambiguous or reasoning-heavy steps delegate to an LLM agent. Example: An invoice processing pipeline where OCR extraction is a deterministic workflow step, but dispute resolution routes to an agent for nuanced reasoning. ---

quiz.question: How do you explain agents vs chatbots to a non-technical stakeholder?
options: When the chatbot: Needs to take actions (send emails, query DBs, call APIs); Handles multi-step tasks spanning >1 response; Must adapt to different paths based on data it retrieves.
Reflexion adds a fourth step: Reflect — after completing a task, the agent reviews whether its answer was correct, identifies mistakes, and stores lessons in memory for…

Measure: Task completion rate — % of tasks completed end-to-end without human intervention; Time savings — Average human time replaced per task; Error rate — Agent errors vs. human errors on same tasks.
A chatbot is like a receptionist who answers questions.
quiz.explanation: A chatbot is like a receptionist who answers questions. An agent is like a project manager who takes your goal, figures out which people (tools) to call, coordinates the work, checks the results, and delivers the final outcome — all without you having to give step-by-step instructions." ---

A thick agent encodes business logic in code (pre/post processing, routing rules) and uses the LLM only where judgment is genuinely needed — more predictable and cheaper. Production recommendation: start thin to validate, then thicken by replacing LLM decisions with coded logic wherever the pattern is consistent. ---
